Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 304 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
WMU 304 is located in the north Porcupine Hills, 
southwest of Nanton, Alberta. It is a large WMU that is 
bordered by highways 22, 2 and secondary road 520 
and the road known locally as the Williams coulee 
road. Portions of the unit lie within the montane, 
foothills fescue and mixed-grass natural subregions of 
Alberta. The easternmost portion contains cropland 
while the majority of the unit consists of rocky ridges 
and forest in the western half of the WMU. WMU 304 
is good habitat for moose, elk, and both deer species. 
WMU 304 was not surveyed specifically for deer or 
moose in the past but has 3 previous surveys for elk in 
the past 25 years in 2007,2015 and 2020. 
Survey Method 
A rotary wing (Astar-B3) transect survey  was 
conducted February 15–17, 2025 flying 26 east-west 
lines at 1.85 km intervals, with 48 per cent coverage 
(800 m wide survey strip, area surveyed 664.8 km2) for 
a total linear survey effort of 831 km. At each 
observation point, ungulates were classified by 
species, and when possible, sex and age were 
recorded.  
Because transects varied in length, the average 
density (R) of mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose 
was calculated by multiplying the number of animals 
per transect (Σx) by total area (km2) searched (total 
survey strip area [Σz]) (Jolly 1969, as described in 
Krebs 2014). Average density (R) was multiplied by 
the area (km2) of the WMU (Z) to determine population 
estimates with a 90 per cent confidence intervals. 
Confidence interval width was calculated by 
multiplying the t statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the 
Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error 
(SE; without replacement) of the abundance estimate 
where SE=sq root variance, and variance = N*(N-n)/ 
(n*(n-1))*(Σx2+R2*ΣZ2-2*R*Σxz) with N as the total 
number of possible transects given 100 per cent 
coverage, and n as the number of transects sampled.  
Moos
e and Elk observations made during the survey 
were recorded even if outside of the transect width. 
Moose, mule deer and white-tailed deer data points 
were truncated to 800m strip width for population 
estimates. All elk observations were summed for a 
minimum total count.   
Results 
Mule Deer 
A total of 1219 mule deer were observed on transect 
with an average group size of 8.9 (range 1-72). The 
estimated density was 1.83 mule deer/km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 2828 individuals (90 per 
cent CI 2287 – 3368). A total of 712 mule deer were 
successfully classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio 
was estimated to be 62:100:47. Due to the timing of 
the survey being mid-February, a small amount of 
antler drop had occurred which will affect these ratios. 
White-tailed Deer 
A total of 931 white-tailed deer were observed on 
transect with an average group size of 7.5 (range 1-
49). The estimated density was 1.40 deer/km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 2160 individuals (90 per 
cent CI 1592-2727). White-tailed deer were not 
classified into sex and age cohorts due to extensive 
antler drop having occurred by the time the survey was 
conducted. The 2025 population estimate represents 
the only statistically rigorous method employed for 
white-tailed deer in WMU 304.  
Moose 
A total of 177 moose were observed on transect with 
and average group size of 1.8 (range 1-7). The 
estimated density was 0.26 moose/ km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 405 individuals (90 per cent 
CI 292 - 520). Moose were generally counted 
anecdotally in past surveys for a minimum total count, 
which likely greatly underestimated the population. 
Elk 
A
 total of 1497 elk were observed with an average 
group size of 59 (range 1-242). The bull:cow:calf ratio 
was found to be 10:100:24. The past surveys are 
presented in Table 1. The elk population appears to be 
similar to the results from 2020 and is, therefore, 
considered steady for the past 5 years.
